speaker: vimo
text: Oops! Soft landing... mostly. Hi! I'm VIMO. I'm an astronaut, and I look after some very special friends. They live far, far away.

speaker: kid
text: Wait, VIMO, who lives up there?

speaker: vimo
text: Machines! Cameras, landers, rovers, even a helicopter. NASA sent them to the Moon and Mars to explore. When their work was done, they stayed there.

speaker: vimo
text: Some people call them space junk. I don't. Each one has a story: where it went, what it did, and what it taught us. Tonight, you and I will visit them. Ready?

speaker: vimo
text: Hold on tight! Three... two... one... lift-off! Our first stop is 1964, when NASA was still learning how to even reach the Moon.

speaker: vimo
text: Every glowing pin is a machine NASA sent out there. Watch them appear, year by year!

speaker: vimo
text: Up here on the Moon: cameras that crashed on purpose, landers, and three cars!

speaker: vimo
text: Mars is much farther. Rovers, landers, parachutes and even a little helicopter live here.

speaker: vimo
text: And some never landed at all. They're still flying away from the Sun. Even my jetpack can't catch them!

speaker: vimo
text: Big question: how did we learn to land on the Moon, and what still works there today?

speaker: vimo
text: Meet Ranger 7! In 1964, nobody had ever seen the Moon up close. So NASA sent a camera... and let it crash.

speaker: kid
text: Crash? On purpose?!

speaker: machine
text: Click! Click! Click! I took pictures all the way down. I didn't need to land. I just needed to look!

speaker: vimo
text: In its last 17 minutes, Ranger 7 sent more than 4,000 photos. They were the closest pictures of the Moon anyone had ever seen.

speaker: vimo
text: See? The closer you get, the more you can see.

speaker: vimo
text: Scientists even gave the place a new name: the Sea that has Become Known. Ranger 7 is still there, in pieces, right where it learned the Moon's first secrets. Thank you, Ranger 7!

speaker: machine
text: Touchdown! And look: my feet are on top of the dust, not under it. The ground is strong!

speaker: vimo
text: Surveyor 1 was America's first soft landing on the Moon. It sent more than 11,000 photos. Now NASA knew: people could land here too.

speaker: vimo
text: So that's how rockets slow you down.

speaker: vimo
text: This is Surveyor 3. It landed in 1967, dug the Moon's soil with a little scoop, and sent photos home. Then it went quiet. Alone. For two and a half years.

speaker: machine
text: ...beep... is anyone... coming?

speaker: vimo
text: Then, in November 1969, Apollo 12 landed close by. Two astronauts walked over to say hello!

speaker: machine
text: Visitors! I knew someone would come back.

speaker: kid
text: Why did they take its camera?

speaker: vimo
text: To see what two and a half years on the Moon does to a machine. Its parts came home for scientists to study. Surveyor 3 helped us twice!

speaker: machine
text: I landed so precisely that the astronauts could walk to an old robot parked nearby.

speaker: vimo
text: Apollo 12 also left a science station. When its top part was crashed into the Moon later, the Moon 'rang' like a bell for nearly an hour!

speaker: vimo
text: So that's how we listen to the inside of the Moon.

speaker: vimo
text: This is it. July 1969. The first time people walked on another world. And this is their ship, the Eagle.

speaker: kid
text: Hey, half of it stayed behind!

speaker: vimo
text: That's the plan! The bottom half was the launch pad. The astronauts flew home in the top half. The bottom half is still standing there today.

speaker: machine
text: My plaque says: 'We came in peace for all mankind.' I've been holding that message for more than 55 years.

speaker: vimo
text: Most of the machines we visit tonight are finished. But this little box is still working. Right now. Watch!

speaker: machine
text: Ping! Ping! Every beam you send, I send back. Same way, every time!

speaker: vimo
text: Scientists measure how long the light takes. That's how we know the Moon is moving away from Earth, about 3.8 centimetres every year. That's how fast your fingernails grow!

speaker: vimo
text: So that's how light measures the distance to the Moon.

speaker: vimo
text: Boing... boing... And in 1971, astronauts brought a car! It came folded up, like a paper toy.

speaker: machine
text: Battery power, wire-mesh wheels and no road at all. I drove the astronauts about 28 kilometres. Not bad for a car that fits in a suitcase... a big suitcase.

speaker: kid
text: Why mesh wheels and not rubber tyres?

speaker: vimo
text: No air means no air-filled tyres. So its wheels were woven from thin steel wire, like a basket!

speaker: vimo
text: The rover is still parked there, waiting. But Apollo isn't finished yet. More astronauts are coming!

speaker: machine
text: When my fender broke, the astronauts fixed it with duct tape and maps. Good as new!

speaker: vimo
text: Even on the Moon, sometimes the best tool is tape!

speaker: vimo
text: Astronauts fix things with what they have!

speaker: vimo
text: In December 1972, the last astronauts left the Moon. Nobody has walked here since. Not yet.

speaker: kid
text: Not yet? Will people go back?

speaker: vimo
text: NASA is planning to! But first, let's see who is still watching the Moon.

speaker: machine
text: I'm the Moon's photographer. From orbit I can still see the Apollo landers, rover tracks and even footpaths.

speaker: vimo
text: So it's true. They're all still there, right where they finished their work. LRO is still working today.

speaker: vimo
text: The answer so far: robots scouted first, people followed, and the mirrors and LRO still send us science.

speaker: vimo
text: So many friends on the Moon! Now hold on. Our next trip is much, much longer. Next stop: Mars!

speaker: vimo
text: Big question: could Mars once have been a home for tiny life?

speaker: vimo
text: A radio message to Mars takes up to 22 minutes! So nobody can drive a Mars robot with a joystick. The robots have to be smart and careful on their own.

speaker: vimo
text: July 20th, 1976: exactly seven years after Apollo 11 landed on the Moon, Viking 1 landed safely on Mars.

speaker: machine
text: The first thing I photographed on Mars? My own foot. I wanted to check I'd landed on something solid!

speaker: vimo
text: Viking 1 sent the first pictures ever taken on the surface of Mars. It also tested the soil, looking for tiny signs of life.

speaker: kid
text: Did it find aliens?

speaker: vimo
text: No aliens! Scientists still talk about what its soil tests meant. That's okay. In science, 'we're not sure yet' is an honest answer.

speaker: vimo
text: Viking 1 kept working for more than six years. It went quiet in 1982 and is still sitting on that plain. Thank you, Viking!

speaker: vimo
text: After Viking, Mars waited 21 years. Then, on the 4th of July 1997, a new lander arrived. Boing! Boing! Boing! It landed in a ball of airbags!

speaker: machine
text: I'm the first rover on Mars, as small as a microwave oven. I never went more than a few metres from my lander, but I was the first!

speaker: vimo
text: Sojourner was the first rover on another planet. Tiny, but it proved a rover can drive on another planet.

speaker: machine
text: They told me I'd work for 90 days. I just... kept going. I drove more than a marathon: 45 kilometres!

speaker: vimo
text: Opportunity was planned for 90 days and explored for more than 14 years!

speaker: kid
text: What's so special about this rock?

speaker: vimo
text: It has hematite, a mineral that forms in water. So long ago, Mars had water!

speaker: vimo
text: Hematite forms in water. Mars was once wet here!

speaker: vimo
text: In 2018, a huge dust storm covered the whole planet. The Sun was hidden, and Opportunity's solar panels couldn't make power.

speaker: vimo
text: NASA called to it more than 1,000 times. It never answered. But it had done its job, and much, much more.

speaker: vimo
text: Goodbye, Oppy. Built for 90 days, you gave us almost 15 years. You are not forgotten.

speaker: vimo
text: Curiosity is as big as a car, too heavy for airbags. So NASA lowered it on ropes from a flying rocket crane. And look: every landing leaves parts behind, like breadcrumbs.

speaker: machine
text: We protected the rovers through a fiery fall, then dropped away. Now we lie in the dust like a trail of breadcrumbs.

speaker: machine
text: I'm climbing a mountain in an old lake bed, reading Mars's history layer by layer, like pages in a book.

speaker: vimo
text: Curiosity showed that Gale crater once held a lake where tiny living things, microbes, could have lived. And it's still working today!

speaker: machine
text: I put my ear to the ground and heard Mars rumble more than a thousand times.

speaker: vimo
text: InSight recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes and learned about Mars' core. Like a doctor listening to a heartbeat!

speaker: vimo
text: Bit by bit, dust covered its solar panels. In December 2022, InSight went quiet. Thank you for listening, InSight.

speaker: machine
text: Sure, I'm lying in the sand now. But I protected Perseverance on the way down. You're welcome!

speaker: vimo
text: These parts were used only once, for a few minutes. But without them, Perseverance couldn't have landed.

speaker: vimo
text: Psst... the parachute has a secret message hidden in its pattern. Engineers wrote it in computer code. Can you crack it?

speaker: vimo
text: Engineers have fun too!

speaker: vimo
text: This little helicopter is Ingenuity. It weighs about the same as two big bottles of water. Its job: try to fly on another planet. Nobody had ever done that.

speaker: kid
text: But you said Mars has almost no air!

speaker: vimo
text: Right! So its blades spin super fast, about 2,400 times a minute. That's much faster than a helicopter on Earth.

speaker: machine
text: I was supposed to fly 5 times. I flew 72 times!

speaker: vimo
text: The first powered flight on another planet! It was planned for five test flights. It flew 72!

speaker: vimo
text: In January 2024, on its 72nd flight, a blade broke, so it can't fly anymore. But every day it still wakes up, checks itself and saves data for future explorers who come to visit. A little hero, waiting on a sandy hill.

speaker: vimo
text: And Perseverance is still out there, exploring. Keep going, Percy!

speaker: machine
text: I'm collecting pieces of Mars in little tubes, so that one day scientists on Earth can study them.

speaker: vimo
text: Perseverance is searching this old river delta for signs of past life. And it's still working today!

speaker: machine
text: We are ten little tubes of Mars rock, left on the ground on purpose, waiting for a ride to Earth.

speaker: vimo
text: This is the first sample depot on another planet. These tubes aren't abandoned. They're waiting. Just like all our friends.

speaker: vimo
text: The answer so far: Mars once had water and places where life could have lived. The samples may tell us more.

speaker: vimo
text: Mars, thank you! But some machines went even farther. Much, much farther. Ready?

speaker: vimo
text: Big question: how far can a machine we built travel?

speaker: vimo
text: Some machines never landed anywhere. They're still flying away from the Sun! Even my jetpack can't catch them.

speaker: machine
text: 1972... I was the first to fly past Jupiter... I sent my last message in 2003. I'm still flying, quietly.

speaker: vimo
text: Pioneer 10 carries a metal plaque with a drawing that shows where it came from: Earth.

speaker: machine
text: I'm the only visitor Uranus and Neptune have ever had.

speaker: vimo
text: Voyager 2 went into interstellar space in 2018. It's still sending data home today.

speaker: machine
text: Launched in 1977. I'm the farthest thing people have ever made. I carry a golden record with sounds and music from Earth. And yes... I still call home.

speaker: vimo
text: On 18 November 2026, Voyager 1 becomes the first human-made object one light-day from Earth: its signal will take a whole day to reach us! It's in interstellar space, between the stars.

speaker: machine
text: I showed the world Pluto's heart-shaped glacier.

speaker: vimo
text: After Pluto, New Horizons flew past Arrokoth in 2019, the farthest world ever explored up close. It's still working!

speaker: vimo
text: The answer so far: out of the Sun's bubble, one light-day away, and still calling home.

speaker: vimo
text: Look at all our friends! Some still work. Some went quiet. Some were used once, on purpose. But none of them are just junk. Each one taught us something.

speaker: vimo
text: See? Old doesn't mean abandoned. They're resting where they finished their work.

speaker: vimo
text: Perfect landing! See, I'm learning too.

speaker: vimo
text: Next time you look at the Moon, remember: there's a lander's bottom half up there, a car, footprints... and a little mirror that still answers when we call.

speaker: vimo
text: And the story isn't over. In April 2026, four astronauts flew around the Moon, farther from Earth than any humans ever. NASA plans to land people near the Moon's south pole in 2028.

speaker: vimo
text: These machines were brave enough to go first. Maybe one day you'll build the next one. And when it finishes its work, someone like me will come and say thank you.
